title: Building Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers
summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets one server serve many AI applications, so an integration is written once instead of per agent framework. This lesson teaches the protocol as of the 2026-07-28 revision, where there is no initialize handshake and no session, and the official Python and TypeScript SDK v2 lines. It covers transports, OAuth and least privilege, the attacks that matter (confused deputy, token passthrough, injection through tool results), long-running Tasks, large tool catalogs, the registry, testing and versioning, and when not to build a server at all.

blocks.text: Both SDK teams describe the same migration shape in their v2 documentation: the new line implements the latest revision and serves older clients from the same server, and the Python documentation says v1 stays in maintenance for libraries that are not ready to move. The TypeScript documentation says its handler serves older clients statelessly from the same factory by default.

The MCP project's client guidance, written for hosts that connect many servers, recommends progressive discovery and, where a sandbox exists, programmatic tool calling. It notes that OpenAI and Anthropic offer built-in tool search which a host may prefer to a custom implementation.

The official registry names Anthropic, GitHub, PulseMCP and Microsoft among its backers, and tells organizations that need private servers to host their own private registry; such registries can implement the same OpenAPI interface so hosts can consume them; the same page says the official registry's own codebase is not designed for self-hosting, so a private registry implements the same interface rather than running that code.
The Tasks extension text says tasks suit expensive computations and batch processing and map naturally onto external job APIs, which is the shape of a server that wraps a CI system or a data export.

The MCP security guide requires any client that offers one-click local server setup to show the exact command without truncation and to obtain explicit approval before running it, because a local server runs with the client's privileges.

subtopics.title: Hosts, clients and servers: who controls what

blocks.text: MCP joins an AI application to the systems it needs through a small, fixed cast. The host is the LLM application the user talks to: an IDE, a desktop assistant or your own agent runtime. Inside it, a client speaks MCP, and the host runs one client per server it is connected to. The server is the program you build. It exposes capabilities to clients and never talks to the model directly.

This lesson targets the 2026-07-28 revision, which the specification's versioning page lists as the current one as of October 2026. Every protocol statement below names the specification page that makes it, every SDK statement names the SDK documentation, and the dated captions say when a fact was checked.

blocks.legend: One host, one client per server (s12). The local server runs as a subprocess over stdio (s3); the remote server answers HTTP POSTs (s2). The approval gate and the audit log are host features this sketch draws, not required components: the specification only says a human should be able to deny tool calls and that clients should log tool usage (s6). Sources: s12, s2, s3, s6.

blocks.caption: Server primitives and who decides to use them
rows: Functions the model may call; they can have side effects
Data the host chooses to load into context
Reusable templates invoked by name, such as a slash command

blocks.text: Choosing the primitive is the first design decision. The Python SDK documentation offers an analogy: a resource is like a GET that loads data and changes nothing, a tool is like a POST that does work and may have side effects. Because tools are model-controlled, the specification says there should always be a human in the loop with the ability to deny tool invocations. This lesson's rule follows: make anything with a side effect a tool, so an approval point exists, and keep read-only reference data as resources.

blocks.caption: Approval defaults by tool class (this lesson's convention; the specification only says a human should be able to deny tool calls)
rows: No side effect; the log gives the audit trail [s6]
Ask once per task, show the inputs
Clients should show tool inputs before the call [s6]
Ask on every call with the exact arguments
A human can deny the call [s6]

blocks.text: One thing servers can no longer do is call the client. Under the 2026-07-28 revision servers do not initiate JSON-RPC requests: when a tool needs the user's input, it returns a result that asks for it and the client retries. Roots, sampling and logging are deprecated in the same revision: they still work, but new implementations should not add them.

subtopics.title: The 2026-07-28 request: no handshake, no session

blocks.text: Earlier revisions opened every connection with an initialize exchange and, on HTTP, handed out a session id. The 2026-07-28 revision removes both. Every request now carries its protocol version and client capabilities in its _meta field, clients should identify themselves on each request, and servers identify themselves in each result, so the server needs nothing from earlier requests.

A server that has to remember something between calls does it explicitly. It mints a handle, such as a basket id or a workflow id, returns it in a result and receives it back as an ordinary tool argument. For an authenticated server a handle is a name, not a capability: the caller's authorization is checked against it on every call.

blocks.caption: What changed from 2025-11-25 to 2026-07-28, checked as of 2026-10
rows: Removed. Servers must implement server/discover; clients may call it first [s1]
Server-initiated sampling, elicitation and roots requests
The server returns an input_required result; the client retries with its answers [s1, s2]
Not resumable; the client re-issues the request as a new request [s1, s2]
Experimental tasks in the core protocol

blocks.text: On Streamable HTTP every request is a POST that carries the version in a header as well as in the body. The server answers with a single JSON object or with a server-sent events stream scoped to that request, and closing that stream cancels the request. The body stays the source of truth: a server rejects a request whose headers disagree with it, so a gateway and the server never act on different values.

The sequence below follows one tool call from a client that has no token yet, through authorization, to every way the server can answer the retried request. The order of the checks is this lesson's design; the specification fixes the status and error codes, not the order.

blocks.text: Note what is missing: no initialize, no session id, no server-to-client request. Each retry is a complete request, which is why a load balancer can send it to any replica.

subtopics.title: Transports: stdio, Streamable HTTP and hosting

blocks.text: Two transports are standard. With stdio the client launches the server as a subprocess and exchanges one JSON-RPC message per line over its standard streams. With Streamable HTTP the server exposes a single MCP endpoint and every client message is its own POST. The choice decides who can reach the server, how it authenticates callers and how it is operated.

rows.pick_when: A local tool for one user that needs local files or devices; the client launches it and credentials come from the environment [s3, s4].
rows.avoid_when: Several users or teams must share one server with central authentication, rate limits and logs; a subprocess per client cannot give you that (design judgment).
rows.example: A repository helper inside an IDE.

rows.pick_when: A shared, remotely hosted server behind your identity provider; a modern request is self-contained, so any replica can answer it [s2, s9].
rows.avoid_when: Only local access is needed and you do not want to run a network service: you would have to validate Origin, bind to loopback and authenticate every connection [s2].
rows.example: A customer-systems server used by several agents and teams.

rows.pick_when: Only to keep serving older clients next to the new endpoint [s2].
rows.avoid_when: Any new server: it is deprecated and new implementations should not adopt it [s1, s2].
rows.example: Keep the old endpoint until the last old client is gone.

blocks.text: stdio has one hard rule: the server must not write anything to stdout that is not a valid MCP message. Logging goes to stderr. If a stdio server dies, the client should restart it, and because the protocol is stateless the in-flight requests are simply lost and can be retried.

An HTTP server validates the Origin header on every connection and answers 403 when it is present and invalid, which stops DNS rebinding. Run locally, it should bind to loopback, and it should authenticate every connection. The TypeScript handler validates no Host header, no Origin header and no token, so you mount those checks in front of it.

Statelessness changes operations. Any replica behind a plain round-robin load balancer can answer a modern request, and the TypeScript handler builds a fresh server instance per request. Three things are not free: a multi-round-trip retry carries a sealed requestState, so every replica of a scaled-out Python deployment needs the same keys; change notifications need a shared subscription bus; and task calls carry the task id in Mcp-Name so a gateway can route them to the instance that holds the task.

Headers let intermediaries route without parsing JSON: every POST carries MCP-Protocol-Version and Mcp-Method, and tools/call, resources/read and prompts/get also carry Mcp-Name. An intermediary that enforces policy on them should reject a request that lacks the version header instead of trusting it.

subtopics.title: Authorization, least privilege and the attacks that matter

blocks.text: Authorization is optional and applies to HTTP transports. When used, the MCP server acts as an OAuth 2.1 resource server: it validates tokens and never issues them, while the client is an OAuth client acting for the user. A stdio server should not follow this specification and takes credentials from its environment.

blocks.legend: OAuth for a remote MCP server (s4): the server publishes protected resource metadata (RFC 9728) and the client discovers the authorization server from it; the token is requested for this server with the resource parameter. The downstream call with a separate credential is the reading of the rule that servers must not accept or transit other tokens (s4, s5). Sources: s4, s5.

blocks.text: The server must implement protected resource metadata, which lists its authorization servers, and a 401 response points to it in the WWW-Authenticate header. The client then finds the authorization server's endpoints and sends a resource parameter naming this MCP server in both the authorization and the token request. The server must check that a token was issued for it as the audience. How the client obtains its client id is a separate step: the specification now prefers Client ID Metadata Documents and lists Dynamic Client Registration as deprecated.

401 with a WWW-Authenticate challenge carrying resource_metadata

403 with error insufficient_scope and the scope needed

blocks.text: Least privilege is a design of scopes, not a setting. Name the scope the call needs in the challenge, publish only a minimal set in scopes_supported, and ask for more when a privileged tool is first used. The security guide lists publishing every scope and using omnibus scopes such as full-access as common mistakes. Because tools/list may vary with the caller's authorization, a read-only token can simply not see the write tools.

Two attacks come from proxying. Token passthrough means accepting a token that was not issued to your server and forwarding it downstream; the guide forbids it because it bypasses controls that depend on the audience and breaks the audit trail. The confused deputy attack hits an MCP proxy that fronts a third-party API with one static client id: if the third-party authorization server remembers consent in a cookie, an attacker's dynamically registered client can obtain a code without the user's consent. The fix is per-client consent stored by the MCP server and checked before it forwards to the third party.

Handles can be guessed: possession of a state handle is not authentication, so bind it server-side to the verified user. Clients must treat tool annotations as untrusted unless the server is trusted, results from one server are untrusted input to another, and servers must validate inputs, apply access controls, rate limit and sanitize outputs.
Do not forward the token you received. Validate that it was issued for your server, then call the downstream system with a credential of its own.

subtopics.title: Building a server with the Python and TypeScript SDK v2

blocks.text: As of 2026-10 both official SDKs have a v2 line, and both answer older clients from the same server as newer ones. The Python class that tutorials taught for years was renamed, and the old import is gone rather than deprecated, so most v1 samples on the web fail on a fresh install. The table records what the SDK documentation says as of the date in its caption.

blocks.caption: The two SDKs, checked as of 2026-10 against their v2 documentation
rows: pip install mcp installs 2.x; the class is MCPServer in mcp.server [s9]
run() takes the transport options; the same app answers both revisions [s9]
FastMCP became MCPServer and the old import path is removed; a library not ready can cap the dependency below 2 [s9]
@modelcontextprotocol/server; McpServer with registerTool and a Zod schema [s10]
createMcpHandler(factory) builds a fresh server per request [s10]
createMcpHandler replaces the per-request transport and connect() wiring [s10]

blocks.text: Both SDKs derive the contract from the code. In Python the function name, docstring and type hints become the tool's name, description and input schema, so the docstring is text the model reads. A ToolError message reaches the model as a failed result it can react to; any other exception reaches it only as a generic failure, with the traceback in your log. In TypeScript the input is declared with a Zod schema passed to registerTool.

blocks.caption: Python SDK v2: one read-only tool. Run against mcp 2.3.0 on 2026-10-16. The ToolError import path is from the SDK's handling-errors page; the rest follows s9 and s12.
TypeScript SDK v2: the same tool over HTTP. Run in process against @modelcontextprotocol/server 2.3.1 on 2026-10-16; the imports follow the serve-over-HTTP page (s10).

blocks.text: Transport options belong to run() in Python, not to the MCPServer constructor. Synchronous Python tools now run on a worker thread so they do not block the event loop. In TypeScript, register tools inside the factory, never on a shared instance outside it, because the factory runs once per request.
A v1 sample that starts with the old FastMCP import fails on v2. Rename the class and the import, and move transport options from the constructor to run().

Not every call returns in seconds. The Tasks extension lets a server answer with a durable task handle instead of a result: the client polls, can answer questions the job raises, and can resume polling after a disconnect. Tasks left the core protocol in the 2026-07-28 revision and became the official extension io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks, which polls with tasks/get and adds tasks/update for client input.

Both sides opt in. The client declares the extension in its per-request capabilities and the server advertises it through server/discover, and the server decides per request whether to create a task. It must not answer with a task handle until the task is durably created, so that a tasks/get for that id would resolve. Cancellation is cooperative: the server acknowledges it but is not obliged to stop the work.

Terminal; the result is what the call would have returned, including a tool result with isError true
Terminal; only for a JSON-RPC error during execution; the error is attached
Terminal; cancellation is eventually consistent and not guaranteed

blocks.text: The sequence shows the whole life of a task, with every status the client can meet on a poll and the error a poll gets after the server has purged the task.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram autonumber participant C as Client participant S as MCP server participant J as Job system C->>S: tools/call
+ tasks capability S->>J: start job J-->>S: job id S-->>C: task handle
working loop until terminal alt client cancels C->>S: tasks/cancel S-->>C: ack, cooperative else client polls C->>S: tasks/get S->>J: read job state J-->>S: state alt working S-->>C: working else needs input S-->>C: inputRequests C->>S: tasks/update
+ answers S-->>C: ack else completed S-->>C: result else failed S-->>C: error else cancelled S-->>C: cancelled else purged S-->>C: error, not found end end end
blocks.legend: Statuses and methods: s7. A task may be purged after its time to live; a poll then gets an error such as task not found or task expired (s7). The ack after tasks/cancel does not promise a cancelled state; the task may still finish in another terminal state (s7). Clients should persist task ids so that polling survives a crash. Sources: s7.

blocks.text: Support is uneven, so check before you promise it. The Python SDK v2 documentation says it removed the experimental Tasks API and does not implement the extension yet (checked 2026-10-16), and a server may only return a task handle to a client that declared the extension on that request. Where it fits, the extension's own text says tasks map naturally onto external job APIs, such as a CI system or a batch export.

Versioning runs on three independent clocks: the dated protocol revision, the server's own version, and extensions. A client states its revision on every request, and a server that does not support it answers 400 with the list of versions it does support so the client can retry. Extensions are advertised in a capabilities field, and Tasks needs both sides to opt in. The specification now has a feature lifecycle policy with a deprecation window of at least twelve months, and it already lists roots, sampling, logging, the HTTP+SSE transport and Dynamic Client Registration as deprecated.

subtopics.title: Catalogs at scale, the registry and compatibility

blocks.text: A tool catalog is part of the prompt. A host that passes every connected server's tool definitions to the model at the start of each conversation can spend most of the context window on definitions before it reads the user's message. The client guidance recommends progressive discovery: keep definitions out of context, give the model a search tool, and load a full definition only when needed. It suggests switching once definitions take a threshold share of the window, such as 1% to 5%, and names keyword, embedding, subagent and hybrid search as strategies.

What a server author controls is the catalog itself. Return tools in a deterministic order and send ttlMs and cacheScope hints on list results, so clients can cache and prompt caches hit. Hosts should not add or remove definitions mid-conversation, which invalidates the provider's prompt cache. Keep tools few and task-shaped; the lesson on structured outputs and tool calling owns tool schemas and descriptions, and this lesson does not repeat it.

For discovery of servers the official MCP Registry is a metadata repository for publicly accessible servers. A server.json record carries a reverse-DNS name such as io.github.user/server-name, where the package or remote URL is, and how to run it, and namespaces are verified through GitHub or DNS. It points to packages on npm, PyPI or Docker Hub rather than hosting code, and security scanning is left to those registries and to downstream aggregators. As of 2026-10 it is in preview, it does not support private servers, and host applications are meant to consume downstream marketplaces instead of calling it.

blocks.caption: Fields of an internal server catalog (this lesson's convention, built on what the registry and the protocol expose)
rows: Someone answers for the server and its tool descriptions
Where the host connects and how it authenticates
Know which hosts can talk to it

blocks.text: A server written on either SDK answers both eras from one endpoint. A hand-written server that supports only the new revision should answer GET and DELETE with 405 and ignore a Mcp-Session-Id header from older clients. Treat a renamed tool or a reworded description like an API change, because it changes how agents behave (this lesson's rule).

subtopics.title: Testing a server, and when not to build one

blocks.text: Test at four levels. Unit-test the functions behind the tools. Drive the server through a real client in process: in Python you hand the server object to Client, which then needs no subprocess and no port, and the TypeScript handler can be called in process the same way. Open the server in the MCP Inspector, which shows one tab per primitive, and in Python is started with mcp dev. Last, check the wire.

blocks.code:
import pytest
from mcp import Client

from server import mcp


@pytest.fixture
def anyio_backend():
    return "asyncio"


@pytest.mark.anyio
async def test_unknown_order_is_a_tool_error_the_model_can_read():
    async with Client(mcp, raise_exceptions=True) as client:
        result = await client.call_tool("get_order", {"order_id": "nope"})
        assert result.is_error is True
        assert "A-1001" in result.content[0].text
blocks.caption: pytest with the in-memory Client (Python SDK v2); run against mcp 2.3.0 on 2026-10-16. It asserts on the failure message the model would read.
What the Python SDK 2.3.0 returned on the wire (observed by the author on 2026-10-16; not documented behavior)
rows: result complete with the text and a structuredContent copy
Mcp-Name header differs from the body
Protocol version 1900-01-01 in both the MCP-Protocol-Version header and _meta (the header alone gave -32020)
result with isError true, although the tools page lists an unknown tool as a protocol error

blocks.text: The last row is why wire checks pay: an SDK and the specification can differ, and only a request on the wire shows it.

blocks.caption: Build a server, reuse one, or skip MCP, as of 2026-10

rows.pick_when: Several hosts or teams need the same system behind one contract and one trust boundary you control (design judgment).
rows.avoid_when: One agent in one codebase will ever call it; the protocol layer adds work without a second consumer (design judgment).
rows.example: Customer order system used by an IDE assistant and a support agent.

rows.pick_when: A maintained server exists, with namespace-verified metadata in a registry and a remote endpoint behind OAuth [s8, s4].
rows.avoid_when: It needs local access you cannot sandbox or its tool descriptions cannot be vetted; the registry leaves code scanning to others [s8, s5].
rows.example: A vendor's hosted server for its own SaaS product.

rows.pick_when: A single agent and a few functions: register them in the agent framework; see the lesson on structured outputs and tool calling (design judgment).
rows.avoid_when: A second host needs the same integration and would reimplement it (design judgment).

rows.pick_when: The step is deterministic, so code calls the API and the model never has to choose it; see the agent architectures lesson (design judgment).
rows.avoid_when: The model must decide whether and when to call it (design judgment).
rows.example: A nightly export that always runs.

worked_example.title: Seven tools for one customer system: scope step-up and the context budget

blocks.caption: Illustrative assumptions of this example, not measured values and not defaults of any SDK
rows: Read-only tools in the first release
Switch threshold (inside the 1% to 5% range the client guidance suggests)
Tools after a year of growth

items: Start with six read-only tools for the orders system, all needing only the scope orders:read.
Their definitions cost 900 tokens in total at the assumed size.
The switch point is 4,000 tokens, so this host loads every definition up front.
Add one write tool, refund_order, which needs the scope orders:write.
A client holding only orders:read calls it and gets HTTP 403 with insufficient_scope and the scope orders:write.
The client asks the authorization server for a token with both scopes, the user approves, and the retry succeeds.
At forty tools the catalog would cost 6,000 tokens, above the switch point.
The host moves to progressive discovery: a search tool plus the definitions one task needs, about 600 tokens.
